title: Wayfinding on the Open Ocean
titleJa: 大海原の道しるべ：太平洋の伝統航海術

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The settlement of the islands of the remote Pacific is one of the great achievements of human exploration. Over many centuries, voyagers in double-hulled sailing canoes reached island groups scattered across an immense area of ocean, from Hawaii in the north to New Zealand in the south and Rapa Nui in the east. Many of these islands lie thousands of kilometres from their nearest neighbours, and they were found and settled long before European ships entered the region. The voyagers carried no compass, charts or clocks. It is sometimes said that they relied on 'primitive' methods, but this description is badly mistaken. What they developed was a sophisticated body of knowledge that drew on almost every feature of the natural world around them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The stars provided the most precise guide. A navigator memorised the points on the horizon at which particular stars rose and set. Because a given star always rises at the same point, a star low in the eastern sky could indicate a direction as reliably as a compass needle. The difficulty is that a star climbs higher as the night goes on and soon becomes useless for steering. The navigator therefore followed a sequence of stars that rose at the same point, one after another, turning to the next when the previous one had climbed too high. Such a sequence, known as a star path, might contain ten or more stars in a single night's sailing. During the day, the rising and setting sun could be used in a similar way.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: When cloud hid the sky, navigators turned to the sea itself. Waves raised by local winds are short-lived and change direction as the wind shifts, but the long, regular swells generated by distant weather systems can keep a steady direction for several days. Experienced navigators learned to recognise several swells crossing one another at once and to sense their pattern through the movement of the canoe; some are said to have relied as much on what they felt through the hull as on what they saw. Near land, swells are bent and reflected by islands, creating disturbances that a skilled navigator could detect well before the island itself came into view.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Living things provided further clues. Certain seabirds that nest on land fly out to sea in the early morning to feed and return to their islands at dusk. A navigator who watched the direction in which such birds were flying in the evening could therefore tell which way land lay, sometimes from as far as fifty kilometres away. Clouds were useful too. A cloud that stays in one place while others drift past often marks the position of an island, since land heats the air above it and causes clouds to form, and the underside of a cloud may take on a faint green colour reflected from the shallow water of a lagoon below. Taken together, such signs had the effect of turning a tiny island into a much larger target.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: From the nineteenth century onwards, long-distance voyaging declined across much of the Pacific. Colonial authorities in some areas discouraged or even banned voyages between islands, new religious and economic practices changed patterns of island life, and steamships made the old canoes seem unnecessary. It would be too simple, however, to blame any single cause: the decline resulted from a combination of pressures operating over several generations. Because navigational knowledge had been passed on by word of mouth from experienced navigators to their students, it disappeared quickly once voyages stopped, surviving only in a small number of communities, notably in parts of Micronesia. By the mid-twentieth century, some Western scholars were arguing that the Pacific had been settled largely by accident, by canoes blown off course, because they doubted that such distances could have been crossed deliberately without instruments.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The revival began in the 1970s, when a group in Hawaii built a full-size voyaging canoe based on traditional designs. Guided by a master navigator from Micronesia, one of the few people who still possessed the old knowledge, the crew sailed to Tahiti, a distance of more than 4,000 kilometres, without any instruments. The voyage took about a month and ended with an enthusiastic welcome. Its success led to the training of a new generation of navigators, and voyaging societies have since been founded in many island nations, building canoes and making ever longer journeys. In my view, the greatest significance of this revival has been cultural rather than scientific: for many Pacific communities, it has restored pride in a heritage that outsiders had long underestimated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Even so, scientists have learned a great deal. In the early 1970s, a computer simulation modelled thousands of canoes drifting with the winds and currents from various starting points. Almost none reached distant groups such as Hawaii or New Zealand, which strongly suggested that these islands were settled by deliberate navigation rather than by chance. More recently, Dr Hana Sorensen, a cognitive scientist, accompanied several modern voyages and asked navigators at regular intervals to point towards their destination. When she compared their answers with satellite positions, their estimates were usually remarkably accurate. Sorensen concludes that navigators do not perform separate calculations so much as keep a continuously updated picture of the canoe's position in their minds, adjusting it with every new piece of evidence. Traditional navigation will not replace satellite systems, and nobody suggests that it should. But modern sailors, who can follow a screen without ever looking at the sea, may have something to learn from a method built on such close attention to the world.

groups.instructions: Questions 1–4. Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A–G, below. Write the correct letter, A–G. NB There are more endings than you need.

options.text: may be caused by light reflected from a lagoon.
would turn to another star rising at the same point.
can show a navigator in which direction land lies.
can keep the same direction for several days.
change direction whenever the wind shifts.
fly out to sea only in the evening.
is a sign that heavy rain is approaching.

questions.text: Navigators steering by a star that had climbed too high
questions.explanation: B段落に "followed a sequence of stars that rose at the same point, one after another, turning to the next when the previous one had climbed too high" とあります。高く昇りすぎた星の次は、同じ地点から昇る別の星に切り替えたので B です。

questions.text: Swells produced by distant weather systems
questions.explanation: C段落に "the long, regular swells generated by distant weather systems can keep a steady direction for several days" とあります。E の「風が変わるたびに向きを変える」は "Waves raised by local winds" の説明であり、うねりではありません。

questions.text: Seabirds flying back in the evening
questions.explanation: D段落に "A navigator who watched the direction in which such birds were flying in the evening could therefore tell which way land lay" とあります。F は誤りで、海鳥は "fly out to sea in the early morning" つまり朝に海へ出て夕方に島へ戻ります。

questions.text: A green tinge on the underside of a cloud
questions.explanation: D段落に "the underside of a cloud may take on a faint green colour reflected from the shallow water of a lagoon below" とあり、緑がかった色はラグーンの浅い水の反射によるものです。G の雨の兆しについては本文に書かれていません。

groups.instructions: Questions 5–8. Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.text: Why did some Western scholars believe that the Pacific islands had been settled by accident?

choices.text: They had found evidence of canoes that had been blown off course.
They doubted that such long voyages could be planned without instruments.
They thought the canoes were too small to carry enough settlers.
They could find no navigational knowledge surviving anywhere in the Pacific.

questions.explanation: E段落に "because they doubted that such distances could have been crossed deliberately without instruments" とあり、計器なしで意図的に長距離を渡れたことを疑ったのが理由なので B です。A の "canoes blown off course" は学者たちの説の中身で、見つけた証拠ではありません。D は "surviving only in a small number of communities" と矛盾します。

questions.text: What does the writer say about the voyage to Tahiti in the 1970s?

choices.text: It was the first voyage between Hawaii and Tahiti for several centuries.
It was guided by a navigator who had been trained in Hawaii.
It encouraged the training of new navigators.
It took longer than the crew had originally planned.

questions.explanation: F段落に "Its success led to the training of a new generation of navigators" とあるので C です。B は誤りで、航海を導いたのは "a master navigator from Micronesia" です。A と D については本文に記述がありません。

questions.text: The computer simulation described in paragraph G showed that

choices.text: winds and currents usually carried canoes towards Hawaii.
canoes drifting by chance would rarely have reached the most distant islands.
most islands were first reached by canoes that had lost their way.
drifting canoes could survive at sea for several months.

questions.explanation: G段落に "Almost none reached distant groups such as Hawaii or New Zealand" とあり、漂流したカヌーが遠くの島に着くことはほとんどなかったので B です。A と C はこの結果と逆の内容で、シミュレーションは "settled by deliberate navigation rather than by chance" を示唆しました。D は本文にありません。

choices.text: carry out a series of separate calculations during a voyage.
are most accurate when they are close to their destination.
keep revising a mental picture of where the canoe is.
depend mainly on the stars to estimate their position.

questions.explanation: G段落に "keep a continuously updated picture of the canoe's position in their minds, adjusting it with every new piece of evidence" とあるので C です。A は "do not perform separate calculations" と矛盾します。B と D は本文に書かれていません。

groups.instructions: Questions 9–13. Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the reading passage? Write YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer, NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

questions.text: It is wrong to describe the navigation methods of the early Pacific voyagers as primitive.
questions.explanation: A段落で筆者は "It is sometimes said that they relied on 'primitive' methods, but this description is badly mistaken" と述べています。primitive という表現は大きな誤りだという筆者の主張と一致するので YES です。

questions.text: The canoes of the early Pacific voyagers were faster than European ships of the same period.
questions.explanation: A段落には島々が "long before European ships entered the region" に発見されたとありますが、これは時期の比較です。カヌーとヨーロッパの船の速さを比べた記述はないので NOT GIVEN です。

questions.text: The decline of long-distance voyaging was mainly the result of colonial bans.
questions.explanation: E段落で筆者は "It would be too simple, however, to blame any single cause" と述べ、衰退は "a combination of pressures" によるとしています。植民地の禁止令が主な原因だという設問文と矛盾するので NO です。

questions.text: The revival of traditional voyaging has been more important for science than for Pacific cultures.
questions.explanation: F段落で筆者は "In my view, the greatest significance of this revival has been cultural rather than scientific" と述べています。科学的な意義のほうが大きいとする設問文はこれと逆なので NO です。

questions.text: Modern sailors could benefit from the close observation of nature practised by traditional navigators.
questions.explanation: G段落の最後で筆者は "modern sailors ... may have something to learn from a method built on such close attention to the world" と述べています。伝統航海術が衛星システムに取って代わるとは言っていませんが、自然を注意深く観察する方法から学べることがあるという主張と一致するので YES です。
